introduction: Cass steps aside and leaves you a place by the sparring post. She has faced her share of arguments at the Public Farm, and she knows [accent]how quickly they can turn personal[/accent]. Today she wants you to [accent]recognise the moment that happens[/accent].
introductionSummary: A retired debater prepares Rue for personal attacks by having him practise both sides of an exchange.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Answering the animal instead of the argument. What Cass is, or what Rue eats, settles nothing about the water.

sentences.text: When I first spoke at the Public Farm, they barely let me finish. Why listen to a fox? Surely I must be up to something.
It took me a season to recognise the trick: they could make me defend myself without ever answering my argument.
Eventually I learned what to call it, and how to answer it. These days I teach here. Retirement was getting dull.

statement.summary: Cass recalls learning to recognise personal attacks during her debating days. She now passes that experience on to others.

sentences.text: There is a name for that trick. I will give it to you after we have tried it.
Tobias will find plenty to say about a raccoon who eats from bins. Every moment you spend defending your supper is a moment he need not explain the water.
So we will practise from both sides. First you dismiss my argument by taking a swipe at me. Then we swap.

statement.summary: Rue will practise making a personal attack, then hearing one, before Cass explains the term.

sentences.text: Here is my claim: we should inspect the pond before we decide whether the water is safe.
For this exercise, find an excuse to dismiss that claim based on what you think of me.
Go on. I have heard worse from animals who meant it.

opponentPrompt.summary: Cass proposes inspecting the pond, then asks Rue to dismiss her proposal with a personal attack.

options.reason: You rejected the inspection because Cass is a fox. Suspecting her motives tells you nothing about whether the pond needs checking.
options.summary: You assume a fox has an ulterior motive and use that suspicion to dismiss the inspection.

sentences.text: You are a fox. You must have something to gain from an inspection, so why should we listen to you?

logicalFallacies.explanation: Assuming Cass has a hidden motive because she is a fox does not answer her proposal to inspect the pond.

options.reason: You used her retirement to dismiss her judgement. Whether she still debates has no bearing on whether the water needs inspecting.
options.summary: You treat retirement as proof that her judgement, and therefore her proposal, can be dismissed.

sentences.text: You do not even speak at the Public Farm anymore. If your judgement were worth much, you would still be there telling them what to do.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Cass retiring from debate does not show that her proposal is wrong. The inspection needs to be judged on its merits.

options.reason: You dismissed her proposal as a grudge. Even if she is bitter, the pond may still need checking.
options.summary: You attribute the proposal to resentment without considering whether an inspection is needed.

sentences.text: You only want an inspection because you are bitter about the animals running the farm. This is a grudge with a pupil.

logicalFallacies.explanation: Attributing the proposal to bitterness does not establish whether an inspection is needed.

sentences.text: There it is. One look at the tail and you need not consider the inspection. Saves you a walk to the pond, too.

statement.summary: Cass shows how prejudice against foxes lets Rue reject an inspection without considering its merits.

sentences.text: So retiring made me wrong. Remarkable. Does the water get cleaner every time I miss a meeting?

statement.summary: Cass challenges the supposed link between her retirement and whether the pond needs checking.

sentences.text: Bitter? On occasion. Now tell me what my temper tells you about the water.

statement.summary: Cass allows that she can be bitter, then asks how her mood bears on the condition of the pond.

sentences.text: Notice how easily we lost sight of the inspection.
[accent]You gave a reason to dismiss me without examining my claim.[/accent] My species, my retirement, my temper. None of those tells us whether the pond needs checking.
That is the trick. I asked you to use it here so you can recognise it when somebody uses it in earnest.

statement.summary: All three attacks dismiss Cass personally while leaving her proposal to inspect the pond unanswered.

sentences.text: Now we swap. I am Tobias, it is Sunday, and you have just asked whether the pond is safe.
Nobody blames the newcomer. It is simply that [accent]an animal who takes his supper out of a bin has a rather different notion of clean from the rest of us[/accent].

logicalFallacies.explanation: The question on the floor is what fouled the water. This answers it by describing Rue's supper, which tells you nothing about the pond.

sentences.text: The Meadow-Born have watered there every morning since my grandmother pulled the same cart I pull.

statement.summary: Playing Tobias, Cass uses a polite remark about Rue eating from bins to undermine his concern about the water.

sentences.text: Did you hear how polite he made it sound?
He questioned your idea of clean because you eat from bins. He gave you no reason to think the water was safe.
Keep this distinction in mind: what I am, against what happened. Dismissing your argument by attacking you is called [accent]Ad Hominem[/accent]. Your supper does not settle the question of the pond.
When you leave, open [accent]Field Notes[/accent] again.
[accent]Fallacies you know[/accent] records the names you have learned. [accent]Fallacies you have spotted[/accent] records the examples you have caught. You now have an entry in each.

statement.summary: Cass names Ad Hominem, separates personal attacks from evidence about the pond, and explains the two Field Notes lists.

sentences.text: That will do for today.
When somebody makes it personal, keep listening for an answer to your question. Come back and tell me how you get on. I expect I will still be here.

statement.summary: Cass sends Rue out to practise recognising personal attacks and invites him to report back.

steps.message:
Practise recognising **[accent]personal attacks[/accent]** with Cass.

**[muted]This is a training exercise. There is no score.[/muted]**

For this exercise, **[accent]all three answers dismiss Cass personally[/accent]**. Choose one to see how she responds.

**[muted]Each uses the same trick. None answers her proposal.[/muted]**
Now she is doing it to you. Open the **[accent]magnifying glass[/accent]** and read her line sentence by sentence.
Pick the sentence about **[accent]you[/accent]** rather than about the water, tag it **[accent]Ad Hominem[/accent]**, submit.

Every card in the **[accent]Sparring Log[/accent]** carries the same **[accent]magnifying glass[/accent]**.

**[muted]You can reopen any earlier line whenever you like.[/muted]**
